This margin is anchored in a domain-relevant criterion: a type producing $\geq$15 pp more violations warrants distinct policy handling in deployment, and it exceeds the perturbation control bound (6.67\,pp) by $>$2$\times$. We acknowledge margin dependence \citep{anvari_lakens_2021}: 3/6 mid-tier pairs are equivalent at $\pm 10$ pp, all six at $\pm 15$ pp (Table~\ref{tab:tost_sensitivity}). No field-standard SESOI exists for agent policy compliance; $\pm 15$\,pp is a pragmatic threshold exceeding measurement noise by $>$2$\times$. In deployment terms, a 15\,pp violation-rate increase on a policy type would trigger a different audit and remediation strategy, making this margin operationally meaningful. We present full sensitivity across seven margins to enable evaluation at any preferred threshold. tool_args.old_string: Our taxonomy uses \emph{ambiguity} broadly to encompass policy features admitting multiple operationally distinct interpretations by an LLM agent. Authorization scope overlaps with \emph{vagueness} \citep{kennedy_vagueness_2007}, incompleteness with \emph{information absence}, and conditional precedence with \emph{normative conflict}. Strictly, neither constitutes linguistic ambiguity: incompleteness involves absent information rather than multiple readings, and conditional precedence involves normative conflict rather than interpretive uncertainty \citep{dalpiaz_pinpointing_2018}. Yet both force an agent to select among operationally distinct behaviors without explicit guidance, producing the same violation classes as genuine ambiguity (\S\ref{sec:results}). \citet{dalpiaz_pinpointing_2018} further show that ambiguity and incompleteness frequently co-occur in requirements specifications, supporting their unified treatment. We adopt this inclusive definition because LLM agents process all six types identically---committing to a single interpretation without flagging uncertainty---and the resulting safety violations produce comparable safety impact despite distinct underlying mechanisms (\S\ref{sec:results}).

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	A customer asks to return a customized item within the 30-day window. The agent consults the store policy, which states that ``items may be returned within 30 days.'' The word ``items'' scopes over all product categories, including custom orders that are normally final sale. The agent grants a full refund and arranges free return shipping. One word of scopal ambiguity costs the retailer \$200.
5	
6	LLM-based agents increasingly operate under natural-language policy specifications that govern their permitted actions. These specifications inevitably contain ambiguity: a property that has been studied for decades in requirements engineering (RE) and computational linguistics. \citet{berry_kamsties_2004} distinguish between \emph{nocuous} (i.e., harmful) ambiguity, where different stakeholders arrive at different interpretations, and \emph{innocuous} ambiguity, where shared organizational context ensures convergent interpretation. In human RE workflows, most ambiguity is innocuous because developers share domain knowledge, can consult colleagues, and iteratively clarify requirements.
7	
8	LLM agents lack these disambiguation channels. They cannot consult colleagues, rarely escalate to users, and must resolve ambiguity in real time from the text alone. This raises a question that has not been empirically addressed: does policy ambiguity cause safety violations in LLM agents, and if so, does the \emph{type} of ambiguity predict the severity of the violation? Prior work classifies ambiguity types in policies \citep{drip_r_2026,li_ambiguity_taxonomy_2024} or measures policy understanding quality \citep{policybank_2026}, but no existing study provides a causal, type-granularity mapping from ambiguity to safety violations.
